_help: Skills for step 8. careers: CEI careers whose training builds this skill directly (recommended when the visitor picks the skill). match: words looked for in a career's skills, duties and tools; a matching training already related to the visitor's majors, minors, interests or careers ranks higher. all: every CEI job-title training teaches this skill, so any training already related to the visitor gets a small boost. tips: how to start building the skill (shown on the results page and /skills-to-learn/ pages).

skills.name: Communication
skills.blurb: Explaining ideas clearly in writing and in person, listening well and adjusting to your audience.
skills.why: Almost every job description lists communication. It shapes interviews, teamwork, customer trust and promotions.
tips: Practice short written updates: what happened, what is next, what you need
Present in class, at work or in a club whenever you can
Learn the vocabulary of the field you want to join so you can speak its language

skills.name: Leadership
skills.blurb: Setting direction, motivating people and taking responsibility for results.
skills.why: Leadership skills help you move from doing the work to coordinating it, and they matter long before you hold a manager title.
tips: Lead a small project, shift or student group
Learn how supervisors plan work, delegate and give feedback
Study the career ladder in your field so you know what the next role requires

skills.name: Critical thinking
skills.blurb: Weighing evidence, spotting assumptions and making sound judgments.
skills.why: Employers value people who can evaluate information and make good decisions without needing every answer handed to them.
tips: Ask why a procedure is done the way it is
Compare two sources before you accept a claim
Practice with case studies and scenario questions in your field

skills.name: Problem solving
skills.blurb: Diagnosing what went wrong and finding a workable fix.
skills.why: Troubleshooting is at the heart of technical, healthcare and service jobs alike, and it is one of the most transferable skills you can build.
tips: Learn a step-by-step troubleshooting method for your field
Keep notes on problems you solve and what worked
Take on tasks where you have to figure out the cause, not just follow steps

skills.name: Computer skills
skills.blurb: Using office software, spreadsheets, databases and the systems your industry runs on.
skills.why: Nearly every role now runs on software, from electronic health records to warehouse scanners and project tools.
tips: Get comfortable with spreadsheets: formulas, sorting and simple charts
Learn the main software used in your target field
Practice touch typing and file organization

skills.name: Artificial intelligence
skills.blurb: Understanding how AI and data tools work and using them responsibly at work.
skills.why: AI tools are spreading into most industries. Knowing how data, automation and AI fit into a job helps you use them well and judge their output.
tips: Learn the basics of data: how it is collected, cleaned and analyzed
Try AI tools on low-risk tasks and check their output carefully
Learn your field's rules on privacy and data security before you use AI with real information

skills.name: Project management
skills.blurb: Planning work, managing schedules and budgets and keeping people coordinated.
skills.why: Projects exist in every field: construction jobs, IT rollouts, marketing campaigns and clinic upgrades all need someone who can plan and deliver.
tips: Break a goal into tasks, owners and dates
Learn common project tools such as task boards and Gantt charts
Track a real project from start to finish and note what you would change

skills.name: Workplace safety
skills.blurb: Recognizing hazards, following safety rules and helping keep coworkers safe.
skills.why: Safety knowledge is required on construction sites, in plants, warehouses and healthcare settings, and employers look for it when they hire.
tips: Learn the main hazards in your target field and how they are controlled
Understand OSHA's role and the safety training your industry requires
Practice using safety data sheets and personal protective equipment correctly

skills.name: Customer service
skills.blurb: Helping customers, patients and clients and solving their problems politely.
skills.why: Customer service skills apply in healthcare, retail, hospitality, trades and offices, and they are often what gets someone hired for a first job.
tips: Practice active listening and repeating back what someone needs
Learn to calm upset customers and set clear expectations
Know the products or services in your field well enough to answer questions

skills.name: Technical and hands-on skills
skills.blurb: Using tools, equipment and procedures specific to a trade or technical field.
skills.why: Hands-on technical skills are what employers test for in trades, manufacturing, healthcare and IT roles.
tips: Learn the tools and equipment used in your field and what each one is for
Follow step-by-step procedures exactly, then learn why each step matters
Look for labs, shop classes, apprenticeships or volunteer work to practice

skills.name: Industry-specific knowledge
skills.blurb: Knowing the vocabulary, regulations, roles and daily work of a specific field.
skills.why: Understanding how an industry really works helps you choose the right path, interview with confidence and get up to speed faster in a new job.
tips: Learn the key terms people in the field use every day
Read job descriptions to see the duties and credentials employers ask for
Talk with people who do the work, or shadow them if you can

skills.name: Professional development
skills.blurb: Building a resume, interviewing, networking and planning your next step.
skills.why: Job search and workplace skills help you turn your education into opportunities and keep growing once you are hired.
tips: Keep a running list of projects, skills and results for your resume
Practice common interview questions for your target job
Set one learning goal for each semester or quarter
